latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Effective viable gram-negative bacterial load disseminating from the primary focus into bloodstream and tissues; drives all downstream signaling and is suppressed by source control plus active antibiotics

TLR4/MD2 recognition of lipopolysaccharide triggers macrophage and dendritic-cell activation, NF-kB signaling, and the cytokine surge (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) that produces fever, vasodilatation, capillary leak, and the dysregulated host response defining sepsis
Hepatic acute-phase reprogramming driven by IL-6 (and to a lesser extent IL-1, TNF); produces CRP, procalcitonin, fibrinogen rise, hypoalbuminemia, and ferritin elevation

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Sepsis-induced endothelial activation and consumptive coagulopathy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: TNF/IL-6 and LPS upregulate endothelial tissue factor, downregulate thrombomodulin and protein C, activate complement and neutrophil NETs, producing widespread microvascular thrombosis and consumptive coagulopathy that may evolve into overt DIC

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Tissue ischemic injury from hypoperfusion and microthrombosis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Combined macrocirculatory hypotension, capillary leak, microthrombi, mitochondrial dysfunction, and oxygen-extraction failure produce organ-level ischemic injury manifesting as lactic acidosis, AKI, hepatic dysfunction, and altered mentation

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Demand-driven neutrophil release and left shift
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Bone-marrow demargination and accelerated granulopoiesis driven by G-CSF, IL-6, TNF; produces neutrophilia with toxic granulation, left shift, and band forms; exhaustion can flip to neutropenia in severe disease or bone-marrow-suppressed hosts

An undrained or unrelieved focus (obstructed urinary tract, cholangitis with biliary obstruction, abscess, infected catheter, perforated viscus) sustains pathogen burden despite antibiotics and is a primary driver of treatment failure and mortality
Pathogen-intrinsic resistance (ESBL, AmpC derepression, carbapenemase, fluoroquinolone resistance) that nullifies portions of empiric coverage and prolongs the time-to-active-therapy interval

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Cumulative injury from delayed effective therapy
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Each hour of inactive antibiotic therapy or unrelieved source in septic shock increases mortality by ~4-8%; this latent variable accumulates ischemic and inflammatory injury that becomes irreversible after a critical threshold
Late-phase CARS-like state with monocyte HLA-DR downregulation, lymphocyte apoptosis, T-cell exhaustion; predisposes to secondary nosocomial infections and reactivation of latent viruses

Severe gram-negative sepsis can drive a secondary HLH/MAS-like state with hyperferritinemia, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and hepatic dysfunction; subclinical pressure exists in many critically ill patients without meeting full HLH criteria

TNF/IL-1 from activated macrophages drive hepatic IL-6 release and acute-phase reprogramming
TNF/IL-6 and direct LPS effects induce endothelial tissue factor, suppress protein C/thrombomodulin, and activate platelets and complement
G-CSF, IL-6, TNF drive bone-marrow demargination and granulopoiesis
Microvascular thrombosis adds to vasoplegia and mitochondrial dysfunction to produce tissue ischemia
iNOS-derived NO causes vasoplegia, capillary leak reduces effective volume, and mitochondrial uncoupling impairs O2 utilization
Undrained focus continuously seeds the bloodstream regardless of antibiotic activity

mechanism_edges.conditionality: active only when initial empiric regimen does not cover the resistance phenotype
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Inactive empiric therapy permits ongoing replication; resistance translates to clinical failure when concordance is absent
Each hour of inadequate perfusion or inactive coverage accumulates irreversible mitochondrial and parenchymal injury
Sustained IFN-γ/IL-18 in severe sepsis can shift macrophage state toward MAS-like hyperactivation in a subset of patients
Compensatory anti-inflammatory programs and lymphocyte apoptosis follow the initial cytokine surge

mechanism_edges.conditionality: elderly, cirrhotic, uremic, or steroid-treated patients may instead develop hypothermia

mechanism_edges.conditionality: may instead show leukopenia in severe sepsis, neutropenic hosts, or older / cirrhotic patients - both extremes meet sepsis criteria

mechanism_edges.conditionality: acute-phase rise dominates early; consumption drops fibrinogen below baseline only in overt DIC
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Consumption in DIC eventually overwhelms acute-phase synthesis; falling fibrinogen is an ominous sign

mechanism_edges.conditionality: purpura fulminans most prominent with N. meningitidis but also seen with severe gram-negative bacteremia, especially asplenic hosts
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Capillary microthrombosis with secondary hemorrhage produces petechiae and purpura

mechanism_edges.conditionality: yield higher when drawn before antibiotics and with adequate volume (40-60 mL across 2-3 sets)

Quantitative or time-to-positivity reflects systemic load; shorter time-to-positivity correlates with mortality
Higher load and persistent bacteremia speed MALDI-TOF or rapid molecular identification

supportive_care: Hour-1 sepsis bundle: lactate measurement, blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4, vasopressors to MAP ≥65 if fluid-refractory
Source identification within first 6 hours: focused history, exam, urinalysis with culture, chest imaging, and CT abdomen/pelvis when indicated; achieve definitive source control as soon as feasible
Two sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics whenever this does not delay therapy more than ~45 minutes
Lactate clearance monitoring (repeat q2-4h) until normalization; persistent elevation prompts re-evaluation of source control and antibiotic adequacy
Dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness (passive leg raise, pulse pressure variation, IVC ultrasound) rather than fixed CVP targets after initial bolus
Early central venous access for vasopressors and frequent labs; arterial line for hemodynamic monitoring in shock
Renal replacement therapy for refractory metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia, volume overload, or uremia; no benefit from early prophylactic initiation
Lung-protective ventilation (Vt 6 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure ≤30 cm H2O) when ARDS develops; prone positioning for moderate-severe ARDS
Glycemic control targeting 140-180 mg/dL using insulin infusion; avoid hypoglycemia
Stress-ulcer prophylaxis for mechanically ventilated patients or coagulopathy
VTE prophylaxis with mechanical and pharmacologic measures unless contraindicated by bleeding or DIC severity
Early enteral nutrition within 24-48 hours when hemodynamically stable

Daily reassessment of antibiotics for de-escalation based on cultures and susceptibilities; total duration usually 7-10 days for uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia, longer for endocarditis, undrained focus, or persistent bacteremia
Repeat blood cultures 48-72 hours after initiation for persistent fever or hemodynamic instability; persistent gram-negative bacteremia warrants source re-evaluation
Delirium prevention bundle (ABCDEF): daily sedation interruption, spontaneous breathing trials, choice of light sedation, delirium monitoring with CAM-ICU, early mobilization, family engagement
Monitor for sepsis-associated complications: AKI (KDIGO staging), DIC (ISTH score), ARDS (Berlin criteria), secondary HLH (HScore in unexplained hyperferritinemia with cytopenias)
Family discussions about goals of care, especially in elderly or comorbid patients, given high mortality and risk of post-sepsis syndrome
Post-discharge plan addressing post-sepsis syndrome: cognitive impairment, ICU-acquired weakness, depression, increased re-infection risk; outpatient follow-up within 1-2 weeks
